set.name: La Chaumière
set.hook: Dole's starred inn: Laurent Barberot's tasting menu Friday and Saturday, his bistrot La Bagatelle on weekdays.
set.why: A hotel-restaurant with a garden and a pool on the avenue du Maréchal Juin, on the edge of Dole. Joël Césari held the star here for years; when he retired, Laurent Barberot, a Vesoul native who trained with Bernard Loiseau, Laurent Petit and Jacques Chibois and cooked at the Plaza Athénée and La Pyramide, took over (reported May 2025). At the weekend he serves one seasonal menu with Jura touches such as smoked eel, Bresse poultry and Jura cheeses; on weekdays the same room becomes the bistrot.
set.verdict: The third star on the Jura list and the only one where the gastronomic menu runs on two days a week, so plan the grand night for Friday or Saturday. Gault&Millau 2026 gives 13.5/20 and says Barberot is changing the house gradually. The weekday bistrot is the easier, cheaper way in. It is a long drive from Lons for dinner: pair it with Pasteur's Dole by day.
set.signature: The single seasonal tasting menu, with Bresse poultry and Jura cheeses (Friday dinner to Saturday dinner only)
set.caveat: About 50 km north of Lons (A39); the starred menu only Friday evening to Saturday evening, bistrot the rest of the week; phone not verified

set.name: Chez l'Artisan Fromager
set.hook: A cheesemaking family's own counter under the rue du Commerce arcades: Morbier first, then raclette and tomme.
set.why: The Poulet family have made cheese for four generations, and this shop at no. 39 rue du Commerce sells what they make: raclette cheese, tomme du Jura and above all Morbier. It sits under the stone arcades in the middle of Lons, so you can step out of the November rain into the smell of rind and cellar. Jura Tourisme lists it as both shop and producer, and the counter speaks French, German, Spanish and Italian.
set.verdict: The best-evidenced cheese counter in central Lons and the right replacement for a Comté affineur the old guide placed here by mistake. Come for the Morbier, which is the family's own; for a run of Comté ages, the Thursday market stalls may serve you better. Hours conflict and nothing dated 2026 turned up, so check before carrying a cool bag across town.

summit.title: Three stars, three towns
summit.story: The Jura's starred cooking sits on the roads north of Lons, not in the town. In Pupillin, the Ploussard village, Vivien Sonzogni and his partners took over the Grapiot in 2024 and won its first MICHELIN star in March 2026; Gault&Millau singles out the Bresse hen with morels. In Arbois, by the Cuisance, Jérôme Brousseau cooks and Lisa Vuillemin makes the desserts at Le Bistronôme, a Bib Gourmand known for Planches trout with morels in Vin Jaune. In Dole, about 50 km north, Laurent Barberot took over La Chaumière in 2025 and serves its starred menu only from Friday to Saturday evening. Port-Lesney's old two-star table is gone.
summit.where: La Table du Grapiot, Pupillin; Le Bistronôme, Arbois; La Chaumière, Dole

street.title: Market squares, Morbier, chocolate
street.story: The Jura pantry is bought rather than eaten out, and most of it is cheese. In Lons the Thursday market, the largest in the department, runs from about seven to five across two squares, with the food stalls on Place de Verdun in the morning; a smaller organic market fills Cours Sully on Saturday mornings. Under the arcades at 39 rue du Commerce, Chez l'Artisan Fromager sells what the Poulet family make, as they have for four generations: raclette cheese, tomme du Jura and above all Morbier. In the centre at 1 rue Saint-Désiré, Pelen has made chocolate since 1899, roasts its own beans and keeps a tea room upstairs.
street.where: Marché de Lons-le-Saunier, Place de Verdun; Chez l'Artisan Fromager, Rue du Commerce; Chocolaterie Pelen, Rue Saint-Désiré

wine.title: Arbois at table
wine.story: Jura wine is mostly drunk where it is made, and in Arbois it reaches the table with the food rather than over a tasting counter. On avenue Pasteur, La Finette has served Comté fondue and chicken in Vin Jaune at varnished log tables since 1961, from a list that holds only Jura bottles. Across town on Place Faramand, Le Bistrot des Claquets opened in 2010 as a cave à manger: a bar from morning to about nine at night, one dish of the day at noon with a cold buffet, and the wine picked from a shelf of local natural growers. One is the old tavern, the other the growers' own canteen.
wine.where: La Finette, Arbois; Le Bistrot des Claquets, Arbois

quartiers:Place de la Liberté and the ar.name: Place de la Liberté and the arcades
quartiers:Place de la Liberté and the ar.teaser: A long street of 146 stone arcades, rebuilt after the fire of 1637, ending at a clock tower
quartiers:Place de la Liberté and the ar.story: Rue du Commerce is Lons under cover: a run of 146 arcades in pale Jura stone, put back up through the 17th century after the fire of 1637, so you can walk its length dry in November rain. Shopfronts sit deep in the shade of the vaults; at the south end the Tour de l'Horloge, built from the stones of an older watchtower. At no. 24 is the house where Rouget de Lisle was born, and Bartholdi's bronze of him, dated 1882, stands at the Place de la Chevalerie crossroads a few minutes away, right arm raised. It was taken for metal by the occupiers in January 1942.
quartiers:Place de la Liberté and the ar.why: Walk the arcades early, before the shops open, when the vaults are empty and the first light comes in low.

quartiers:Place de la Comédie and the ma.name: Place de la Comédie and the market squares
quartiers:Place de la Comédie and the ma.teaser: Thursday is the day: clothes and tools on one square, cheese and Morteau on the next
quartiers:Place de la Comédie and the ma.story: On a Thursday the centre of Lons turns into the largest market in the department. The food goes up in the morning on the Place de Verdun, the hardware, clothes and household stalls fill the Place du 11 Novembre all day, and the theatre looks down on both: a rococo house rebuilt in 1901 after a fire and restored in 1997. Come with a cool bag and you will hear the plateau and the Bresse in the accents behind the trestles. The layout may change: in June 2026 the new mayor, Cyrille Brero, tested moving the non-food stalls onto Place de la Liberté and rue du Commerce.

curiosities:Arbois in the first gazette.name: Arbois in the first gazette
curiosities:Arbois in the first gazette.teaser: On 15 May 1936 France named its first six AOCs, and Arbois heads the list
curiosities:Arbois in the first gazette.story: The 1935 law created the appellation d'origine contrôlée; the first decrees came on 15 May 1936, a day after the agriculture minister's report on Châteauneuf-du-Pape cleared the way. Six names went through: Arbois, Cassis, Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Cognac, Monbazillac and Tavel. Arbois sits first on the alphabetical list, and from there grew the local line that the Jura holds France's oldest appellation. The campaign behind the law was led by the Rhône grower Baron Pierre Le Roy de Boiseaumarié and the Bordeaux senator Joseph Capus. All six turned 90 in 2026, and INAO marked the anniversary in February.
curiosities:Arbois in the first gazette.why: Read 'Appellation Arbois Contrôlée' on a label as a date: May 1936, among the first six in France.
facts: Any bottle labelled Arbois or Arbois-Pupillin: taste one at Domaine Stéphane Tissot's caveau, 35 Place de la Liberté in Arbois, or order one with lunch at La Finette, whose list is all Jura

Arbois's 'first AOC in France' is a local and guidebook claim; INAO dates all six to the same day, and Châteauneuf-du-Pape points to the minister's report on its case, dated 14 May 1936. The old guide's inclusion of Vosne-Romanée was wrong: the sixth was Cognac

culture:La Maison de la Vache qui rit.name: La Maison de la Vache qui rit
culture:La Maison de la Vache qui rit.teaser: A laughing cow first painted on army supply trucks became a cheese brand born in Lons
culture:La Maison de la Vache qui rit.story: The cow began in the trenches. In the First World War Benjamin Rabier drew a grinning cow for the meat-supply trucks of the unit nicknamed the Wachkyrie, a joke on Wagner's Valkyries. Léon Bel had served with it, and in 1921 in Lons he registered La Vache qui rit for his processed cheese, a fromage fondu. The red cow with the cheese-box earrings followed in 1923 or 1924. The museum on rue Richebourg tells a century of the brand through its design and advertising, and was refreshed for the 2021 centenary.
culture:La Maison de la Vache qui rit.why: Look for the earrings on the old boxes: each one shows the cow wearing her own box.

provisioning:Cancoillotte by the jar.name: Cancoillotte by the jar
provisioning:Cancoillotte by the jar.teaser: A runny, lean Franche-Comté cheese sold cold in pots: protected since May 2022, rare outside the region
provisioning:Cancoillotte by the jar.story: Cancoillotte looks like a pale, glossy custard behind the glass. It is made from metton, a dry skim-milk curd, melted down with water, butter and often garlic or white wine, and it stays runny once cold. Since 20 May 2022 the name has been an EU-protected IGP, and the trade sold the equivalent of about 25 million pots in 2024, almost all of them close to home. Buy the plain one and one with garlic, check the date, and keep it in the fridge on board.
provisioning:Cancoillotte by the jar.why: Buy a fresh jar from a market stall or fromager, not the supermarket tub, and warm it gently on board.
facts: Melted cheese from metton curd, under 15 % fat, sold in glass jars or tubs; IGP Cancoillotte since 20 May 2022

avoid:Vin Jaune on a café terrace.name: Vin Jaune on a café terrace
avoid:Vin Jaune on a café terrace.teaser: If the 'vin jaune' on the terrace list comes from a 75 cl bottle, it is not Vin Jaune
avoid:Vin Jaune on a café terrace.story: Under the arcades the café boards chalk up 'vin jaune' by the glass, and nobody brings the bottle to the table. That is the problem. Vin Jaune may only be sold in one bottle: the squat 62 cl clavelin, reserved by the appellation rules for the Vin Jaune of Arbois, Côtes du Jura, L'Étoile and Château-Chalon. A pour from a tall 75 cl bottle is something else, often an oxidative Savagnin, a good wine in its own right but not the one on the board. The real thing smells of walnut and curry and is best met with the person who made it.
avoid:Vin Jaune on a café terrace.why: Ask to see the bottle: no clavelin, no Vin Jaune, whatever the board says.
facts: Look for the short-necked 62 cl clavelin on the table or the shelf before you order a glass

avoid:Comté in plastic.name: Comté in plastic
avoid:Comté in plastic.teaser: A vacuum-packed wedge with no age and no affineur teaches you nothing about Comté
avoid:Comté in plastic.story: The souvenir cellars stack pre-cut wedges of Comté in plastic by the till, often young wheels from large-scale affinage, sold with no age on the label and no name behind it. Comté changes completely with time and with the cellar it ripened in: a young piece is milky and soft, an old one dry, nutty and crunchy with crystals. A single anonymous wedge cannot show you that. A fromager-affineur cuts from the wheel in front of you, tells you how many months it has, and lets you taste before you pay.
avoid:Comté in plastic.why: Taste three ages side by side, cut to order, before you buy any of them.
facts: Check the wedge's label for an age in months and the affineur's name; if both are missing, put it back

avoid:Jeunet in Arbois.name: The Jeunet name
avoid:Jeunet in Arbois.teaser: Older guides still print a two-star Maison Jeunet; neither Arbois nor Germigney serves it any more
avoid:Jeunet in Arbois.story: Jean-Paul Jeunet announced his retirement in February 2016 and left the Arbois kitchen to his second, Steven Naessens, who ran it as Maison Jeunet. In November 2021 Naessens took the name and its two Michelin stars to the Château de Germigney at Port-Lesney; the old Arbois house, a Carmelite convent of 1643, became Carmel 1643 (reported 2023). Then in July 2023 Naessens left Germigney too. The château's table has changed hands twice since, and the Jura's tourist board counted three starred tables in March 2026, none of them called Jeunet. Lists and guides, this one's earlier edition included, still print the old name.
avoid:Jeunet in Arbois.why: If a list sends you to a two-star Jeunet dinner, it is out of date: book a starred table that exists now.
facts: At 9 rue de l'Hôtel de Ville in Arbois stands the Carmel 1643 building (2023 report), and at Germigney a new kitchen under another name since September 2026: neither is the old two-star table

listening:No hi-fi listening bar.name: No hi-fi listening bar
listening:No hi-fi listening bar.teaser: No listening bar in Lons, and none we could find in Besançon either
listening:No hi-fi listening bar.story: A listening bar, in the sense the word now carries, is a room built round a serious sound system and a wall of records, where people come to hear albums played through rather than to talk over them. We looked for one in Lons-le-Saunier and in Besançon in October 2026 and found none; in France such rooms are still a big-city idea. The Jura's evening is a different pleasure: a cold cellar, a clavelin opened by someone who can explain it, or a loud night at the town's own concert hall on the edge of the centre.
listening:No hi-fi listening bar.why: Trade the turntable for the counter, or for the concert hall on a show night.
facts: An evening glass at a counter where the person pouring knows the grower

linger:Café de la Comédie.name: Le Grand Café du Théâtre
linger:Café de la Comédie.teaser: A brasserie bar facing the town theatre since 1847: coffee at the counter, the square going past
linger:Café de la Comédie.story: The old guide put a café under a theatre colonnade on the Place de la Comédie. There is no theatre there now: the square kept the name of a small playhouse of the Revolution years, long demolished. The real theatre stands at the head of the Place de la Liberté, and the café that has faced it since 1847 is the Grand Café du Théâtre, on the corner of rue Jean Jaurès. Expect a long brasserie room with a bar, a terrace, regulars reading the paper over a coffee, and at noon the clatter of steak-frites, tartare and mussels going out.

drink:Poulsard and Trousseau.name: Poulsard and Trousseau
drink:Poulsard and Trousseau.teaser: Two native reds: one pale enough to read through, the other dark, firm and tasting of iron
drink:Poulsard and Trousseau.story: The Jura's own red grapes cover about a fifth of its vines between them, Poulsard (called Ploussard in Pupillin) a little more than Trousseau. Poulsard has thin skins and makes a wine so pale it can pass for a dark rosé: orange-ruby, cranberry and cherry, almost no tannin, bright acid. Pupillin, above Arbois, signs itself the world capital of Ploussard. Trousseau is its opposite, deeper in colour, firmer, black cherry with an iron, peppery edge, and at its best on the gravels around Arbois. Pour them side by side and the Jura's red range is laid out in two glasses.
drink:Poulsard and Trousseau.why: Ask La Finette in Arbois, whose list is all Jura, for one of each, and taste the pale one first.
facts: Poulsard: translucent orange-ruby, red berries, light and acidic, serve at 12 to 14 °C. Trousseau: darker ruby, black cherry, iron and pepper, more grip, serve at 14 to 16 °C

drink:Macvin, Crémant and Marc.teaser: The apéritif made of must and brandy, the everyday sparkling, and the oak-aged digestif
drink:Macvin, Crémant and Marc.story: Three Jura appellations name a product rather than a place. Macvin du Jura, an AOC since 14 November 1991, is a mistelle: unfermented grape must stopped with Marc du Jura, roughly two parts juice to one of brandy, then aged in oak. It comes out sweet, grapey, around 16 percent, and is poured cold before dinner. Crémant du Jura, recognised in 1995, is bottle-fermented sparkling, mostly Chardonnay, nine months at least on its lees: the bubble cellars open at any hour. Marc du Jura, the pomace brandy, became an AOC of its own by decree on 2 February 2015 and closes the meal.
drink:Macvin, Crémant and Marc.why: Start a cellar visit with a Crémant and end it with a thimble of Macvin; it is the Jura's own way into and out of a meal.
facts: Macvin: amber or ruby, raisin and walnut, sweet, about 16%. Crémant: fine bubble, apple and brioche, dry. Marc: amber after oak, dried fruit and fire
Macvin du Jura (blanc, rosé or rouge); Crémant du Jura (brut, often blanc de blancs); Marc du Jura

A Macvin as apéritif, a Crémant brut by the glass, a Marc after the cheese; EUR 14 to 35 a bottle (seen May 2026). Domaine Macle pours both Macvin and Crémant by appointment; the Tissot caveau in Arbois opens with its Crémant Indigène

around:Dole.name: Dole
around:Dole.teaser: A tanner's house on the canal where Pasteur was born, under a 73-metre collegiate tower
around:Dole.story: Dole, the old capital of Franche-Comté, climbs from the Doubs to the Collégiale Notre-Dame, built from 1509 to 1574, its bell tower of 1596 rising 73 metres over the roofs. Below it, the Canal des Tanneurs runs between old tannery houses, water slapping at the stone footings. In one of them Louis Pasteur was born in 1822, the son of a tanner; the house is now a museum of his childhood and family. Note the calendar: the birthplace closed for the winter on 1 November 2026 and reopens in February.
around:Dole.why: The towpath along the Canal des Tanneurs, with the collegiate tower above the rooftops.
